To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) Treg cells are a heterogeneous population of lymphocytes expressing different surface markers; (ii) Treg cells express different isoforms of FoxP3, which are differently regulated during the course of multiple sclerosis; (iii) PD-1 expression is upregulated on Treg cells in multiple sclerosis patients, and this is associated with a reduced suppressive capacity.

(1) FoxP3 isoform expression by CD4+ T cells is different in patients with multiple sclerosis compared to healthy controls; (2) PD-1 is a marker of functional exhaustion in Treg cells; (3) PD-1 expression on Treg cells is higher in patients with multiple scleroses than in controls.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the identification of Treg subsets and the definition of their functional status in MS are critical to the development of new therapeutic approaches.
the identification of the most suppressive and functionally active Tregs may help us in understanding the mechanisms of immune regulation and in developing novel immunomodulatory strategies.
the identification of Tregs is not a trivial task and that the choice of the reagents and the markers used to define Tregs should be made very carefully.
